difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: MODERATE — the relation (a life stage : the stage immediately after it) is quick to spot, but the answer needs the technical name of the adult insect and the rejection of two closely associated distractors (cocoon, nymph); about 1 minute.
concept: Analogy: successive life stages of an insect that undergoes complete metamorphosis (egg, larva, pupa, imago).
stem:
Select the option that best completes the analogy.

*Egg* : *Larva* :: *Pupa* : ________

options.label: A
options.text: Cocoon

options.label: B
options.text: Nymph

options.label: C
options.text: Imago

options.label: D
options.text: Larva

solution.quick: An insect with complete metamorphosis passes through egg, larva, pupa and adult, in that order. *Egg* : *Larva* is (a stage : the stage that immediately follows it), so the blank is the stage after the pupa: the adult insect, called the *imago*.

steps.title: Fix the relation in the given pair
steps.body: In insects such as butterflies, beetles and flies, the larva (for example a caterpillar or a maggot) hatches from the egg. The two words name successive life stages, and the second is the stage that **immediately follows** the first. The relation is therefore (stage : next stage), in that order.

steps.title: Apply the relation to *Pupa*
steps.body: Complete metamorphosis has four stages in a fixed order: egg → larva → pupa → adult. The stage that immediately follows the pupa is the adult, which entomologists call the **imago**. So the blank is *Imago*.

steps.title: Eliminate the remaining options
steps.body: A *cocoon* is the silk case that a larva spins around itself before it pupates; it is a structure, not a life stage. A *nymph* is the juvenile stage of insects with **incomplete** metamorphosis (egg → nymph → adult), which have no pupa at all. *Larva* is the stage **before** the pupa, so it reverses the direction of the relation.

steps.title: Check the direction
steps.body: Egg → Larva and Pupa → Imago are both (stage → next stage) in the same life cycle, so the analogy holds with the order of the terms unchanged.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: A cocoon is the silk casing spun by a larva and inside which the pupa develops. It is closely linked with the pupa but is a structure, not the stage that follows it.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: A nymph is the young stage of insects with incomplete metamorphosis, such as grasshoppers. That life cycle has no pupa, so a nymph never follows a pupa.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: The imago is the adult, sexually mature insect that emerges from the pupa. It is the stage immediately after the pupa, just as the larva is the stage immediately after the egg.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: The larva comes before the pupa. Choosing it gives (stage : previous stage), which reverses the relation of the given pair.

solution.commonTrap: Choosing *Cocoon* because it is the word most strongly associated with the pupa. The given pair links a stage to the **next stage** of the life cycle, and a cocoon is a casing, not a stage.

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: MODERATE — two parallel folds and two edge cuts; the student must work out which edges of the folded strip are creases and which are free ends of the paper, a short but error-prone mapping; about 2 minutes.
concept: Paper folding and cutting: mapping cuts on a folded strip back to the unfolded strip, separating crease edges from free edges.
stem:
A rectangular strip of paper lies in a fixed plane and occupies the region $0 \le x \le 24$, $0 \le y \le 6$ (all lengths in cm). It is folded twice, and both fold lines are parallel to the $y$-axis.

1. **First fold:** along the line $x = 12$, so that the part with $x \ge 12$ is laid over the part with $x \le 12$.
2. **Second fold:** along the line $x = 6$, so that the part of the folded strip with $x \ge 6$ is laid over the part with $x \le 6$.

The folded strip now occupies $0 \le x \le 6$, $0 \le y \le 6$ in four layers. Holding all four layers together, two half-discs of radius $1$ cm are cut away: one centred at $(0, 3)$ and one centred at $(6, 3)$, each being the half of the disc that lies inside the folded strip. The strip is then completely unfolded.

How many holes in the unfolded strip are completely surrounded by paper?

solution.quick: Each point $x$ of the folded strip comes from the four original points $x$, $12 - x$, $12 + x$ and $24 - x$. The edge $x = 0$ of the folded strip holds the crease $x = 12$ and the two free ends $x = 0$, $x = 24$; the edge $x = 6$ holds the creases $x = 6$ and $x = 18$. A cut on a crease becomes a full hole and a cut on a free end becomes an edge notch, so there are $3$ enclosed holes (at $x = 6, 12, 18$).

steps.title: Write the unfolding map
steps.body: The first fold sends $x \mapsto 24 - x$ for $x \ge 12$, and the second sends $x \mapsto 12 - x$ for $6 \le x \le 12$. Undoing them, a point at position $x$ ($0 \le x \le 6$) of the folded strip lies over the four original positions $x$, $12 - x$, $12 + x$ and $24 - x$, one per layer.

steps.title: Identify what lies along each cut edge
steps.body: At $x = 0$ the four positions are $0$, $12$, $12$ and $24$: the two short free ends of the strip ($x = 0$ and $x = 24$) and the first crease ($x = 12$, where the layers $12 - x$ and $12 + x$ join). At $x = 6$ the positions are $6$, $6$, $18$, $18$: the second crease $x = 6$ and the crease $x = 18$ (the image of $x = 6$ in the far half).

steps.title: Unfold the cut at $(0, 3)$
steps.body: The half-disc occupies $0 \le x \le 1$ of the folded strip, so it removes paper over $[0, 1]$, $[11, 12]$, $[12, 13]$ and $[23, 24]$ (with $2 \le y \le 4$). The two pieces meeting at the crease $x = 12$ form one full circular hole centred at $(12, 3)$. The pieces at $[0, 1]$ and $[23, 24]$ are half-disc notches on the two short edges; they are open to the outside, so they are not enclosed holes.

steps.title: Unfold the cut at $(6, 3)$
steps.body: This half-disc occupies $5 \le x \le 6$, so it removes paper over $[5, 6]$, $[6, 7]$, $[17, 18]$ and $[18, 19]$. These join in pairs across the creases $x = 6$ and $x = 18$, giving two full circular holes centred at $(6, 3)$ and $(18, 3)$.

steps.title: Count the enclosed holes
steps.body: Full holes are centred at $x = 6$, $12$ and $18$, so the unfolded strip has $3$ holes completely surrounded by paper, plus two semicircular notches at its ends.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: This counts only the two holes made by the cut at $(6, 3)$. The edge $x = 0$ of the folded strip is not made only of free ends: it also contains the crease $x = 12$, so that cut produces a third full hole.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: Full holes appear at $x = 6$, $12$ and $18$, where a cut edge lies on a crease. The remaining two pieces are notches on the free ends $x = 0$ and $x = 24$.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: This treats both edges of the folded strip as pairs of creases, giving two full holes per cut. The edge $x = 0$ holds the two free ends of the strip, which give notches, not holes.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: This counts each of the eight half-disc pieces (four layers times two cuts) as a separate hole. Pieces that meet across a crease merge into one hole, and the pieces on the free ends are open notches.

solution.commonTrap: Assuming that every edge of the folded strip is a fold. After two folds the edge $x = 0$ carries the crease $x = 12$ **and** the two original ends of the strip, so the same cut gives one full hole and two edge notches.

# folded x in [0,6] lies over original x, 12-x, 12+x, 24-x
pre=lambda a,b:[(a,b),(12-b,12-a),(12+a,12+b),(24-b,24-a)]
m=[]
for a,b in sorted(pre(0,1)+pre(5,6)):
    if m and abs(m[-1][1]-a)<1e-9: m[-1]=(m[-1][0],b)  # pieces joined at a crease
    else: m.append((a,b))
holes=[s for s in m if s[0]>0 and s[1]<24]
print(m, len(holes))  # 3 interior full discs at x=6,12,18

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: VERY_HARD — all four sentences sound natural; three hide errors from different areas (a mismatched correlative pair, the past subjunctive after 'it is high time', agreement with 'each' plus an 'as well as' phrase), and the one correct sentence uses a plural verb that many test-takers wrongly change to singular; about 2.5 minutes.
concept: English grammar: correlative conjunctions, the past subjunctive after 'it is high time', and subject–verb agreement with 'each', 'as well as' and 'one of those who'.
stem: Select the sentence that is grammatically correct.

options.label: A
options.text: *Hardly had the auditors left the building than the manager began shredding the files.*

options.label: B
options.text: *It is high time the committee takes a final decision on the merger.*

options.label: C
options.text: *Each of the interns, as well as their mentors, were invited to the annual review.*

options.label: D
options.text: *She is one of those analysts who verify every figure twice before a report is released.*

solution.quick: (A) mixes correlatives: it must be *hardly … when* (or *no sooner … than*). (B) needs the past form after *it is high time*: *took*. (C) has the singular subject *each*, so *was invited*. In (D) *who* refers to the plural *analysts*, so *verify* is correct.

steps.title: Sentence (A): correlative pairs
steps.body: *Hardly* and *scarcely* pair with **when** (*Hardly had X happened when Y happened*); only *no sooner* pairs with **than**. *Hardly had the auditors left … than* mixes the two patterns. Correct forms: *Hardly had the auditors left the building when …* or *No sooner had the auditors left the building than …*. (A) is incorrect.

steps.title: Sentence (B): *it is high time*
steps.body: *It is high time* (like *it is time*) is followed by a clause in the **past** form, even though the meaning is present or future: the action is overdue. The correct sentence is *It is high time the committee **took** a final decision*. The present form *takes* is an error, so (B) is incorrect.

steps.title: Sentence (C): agreement with *each* and *as well as*
steps.body: The grammatical subject is **each**, which is singular; *of the interns* is a prepositional phrase that does not change the number. The phrase *as well as their mentors* is parenthetical and does not join the mentors to the subject the way *and* would. The verb must be singular: *Each of the interns, as well as their mentors, **was** invited*. (C) is incorrect.

steps.title: Sentence (D): *one of those … who*
steps.body: The relative pronoun *who* refers to the nearest plural noun, *analysts*: she belongs to the group of analysts who verify every figure twice. A relative clause takes the number of its antecedent, so the plural **verify** is correct. In the clause *before a report is released*, *is* agrees with the singular *a report*. (D) has no error.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: *Hardly* is paired with *when*, not *than*. The sentence should read *Hardly had the auditors left the building when the manager began shredding the files* (or use *No sooner … than*).

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: After *it is high time*, the verb takes the past form to show that the action is overdue: *It is high time the committee took a final decision on the merger.*

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: The subject is the singular *each*; neither *of the interns* nor the parenthetical *as well as their mentors* makes it plural. The verb should be *was invited*.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: *Who* refers to the plural *analysts*, so the relative clause correctly uses the plural *verify*; *is released* agrees with *a report*. The sentence is grammatically correct.

solution.commonTrap: Rejecting (D) by 'correcting' *verify* to *verifies* because the sentence begins with *She is one*. The verb in the relative clause agrees with *analysts*, the antecedent of *who*, not with *one*.

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: HARD — both the shares and the total change, so each statement needs shares converted to amounts; the traps are reading a falling share as a falling amount, an amount that stays exactly the same, and confusing the largest absolute increase with the largest percentage increase; about 3 minutes.
concept: Data interpretation: converting percentage shares of a changing total into amounts and comparing absolute and percentage changes.
stem:
A research institute divides its annual grant among five laboratories. The total grant was ₹ 450 crore in 2023 and ₹ 540 crore in 2024. The table gives each laboratory's share of the total grant in each year.

| Laboratory | Share in 2023 (%) | Share in 2024 (%) |
|---|---|---|
| Optics | 30 | 25 |
| Genomics | 24 | 19 |
| Robotics | 18 | 16 |
| Materials | 16 | 22 |
| Climate | 12 | 18 |

Consider the following statements about the amounts (in ₹ crore) received by the laboratories.

- **(I)** Exactly one laboratory received a smaller amount in 2024 than in 2023.
- **(II)** Among the five laboratories, Materials had the largest percentage increase in its amount from 2023 to 2024.
- **(III)** Optics received the same amount in both years.

Which one of the following is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Only (I) is true

options.label: B
options.text: Only (I) and (III) are true

options.label: C
options.text: Only (II) and (III) are true

options.label: D
options.text: (I), (II) and (III) are all true

solution.quick: Amount = share × total. In ₹ crore, 2023 → 2024: Optics $135 \to 135$, Genomics $108 \to 102.6$, Robotics $81 \to 86.4$, Materials $72 \to 118.8$, Climate $54 \to 97.2$. Only Genomics fell, so (I) is true; Climate grew $80\%$ against $65\%$ for Materials, so (II) is false; Optics is unchanged, so (III) is true.

steps.title: Statement (I)
steps.body: Only Genomics has a smaller amount in 2024 ($102.6 < 108$). Optics is unchanged and Robotics rose although its share fell, because the total grew by $20\%$. Exactly one laboratory received less, so (I) is **true**.

steps.title: Statement (II)
steps.body: Percentage increases: Materials $\dfrac{46.8}{72} \times 100 = 65\%$; Climate $\dfrac{43.2}{54} \times 100 = 80\%$; Robotics $\dfrac{5.4}{81} \times 100 \approx 6.7\%$. Climate has the largest percentage increase even though Materials has the largest absolute increase. (II) is **false**.

steps.title: Statement (III) and conclusion
steps.body: Optics received $135$ crore in both years, so (III) is **true**. Only (I) and (III) are true, which is option (B).

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: (III) is also true: $30\%$ of $450$ and $25\%$ of $540$ are both $135$ crore. A five-point fall in share is exactly cancelled by the $20\%$ growth of the total.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: Genomics is the only laboratory whose amount fell ($108 \to 102.6$), and Optics stayed at $135$ crore. (II) fails because Climate grew by $80\%$ against $65\%$ for Materials.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: (II) is false and (I) is true. Materials has the largest **absolute** increase ($46.8$ crore), but Climate has the largest **percentage** increase ($80\%$).

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: (II) is false: the percentage increase of Climate ($80\%$) exceeds that of Materials ($65\%$).

solution.shortcut: Amount ratio (2024/2023) $= \dfrac{s_{2024}}{s_{2023}} \times \dfrac{540}{450} = 1.2 \times \dfrac{s_{2024}}{s_{2023}}$. An amount falls exactly when the share ratio is below $\tfrac{5}{6}$: Optics $\tfrac{25}{30} = \tfrac{5}{6}$ (unchanged), Genomics $\tfrac{19}{24} < \tfrac{5}{6}$ (falls), Robotics $\tfrac{16}{18} > \tfrac{5}{6}$ (rises). The growth factors are $1.2 \times \tfrac{22}{16} = 1.65$ for Materials and $1.2 \times \tfrac{18}{12} = 1.8$ for Climate.
solution.commonTrap: Reading the change in **share** as the change in **amount**. Optics, Genomics and Robotics all lose share, but because the total grows by $20\%$ only Genomics actually receives less, and Optics receives exactly the same.

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: HARD — the arithmetic is short, but the student must track how removing one example changes the training-set majority and apply the tie-break rule; the counter-intuitive result (LOOCV error 1 while the training error is 8/17) defeats intuition; about 2 minutes.
concept: Leave-one-out cross-validation of a majority-class baseline: holding out an example shifts the training majority against it.
stem:
A quality team builds a baseline classifier for inspected components. The baseline ignores every input feature and predicts the label that occurs most often in its training set; when the two labels occur equally often in its training set, it predicts *Reject*.

The dataset has $17$ components: $9$ labelled *Accept* and $8$ labelled *Reject*.

The leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) estimate of the misclassification rate of this baseline is

solution.quick: Holding out an *Accept* leaves $8$ *Accept* and $8$ *Reject*: a tie, so the baseline predicts *Reject* (wrong). Holding out a *Reject* leaves $9$ *Accept* and $7$ *Reject*, so it predicts *Accept* (wrong). All $17$ held-out components are misclassified: the LOOCV error is $17/17 = 1$.

steps.title: Set up LOOCV
steps.body: LOOCV runs $17$ rounds. In each round one component is held out, the baseline is 'trained' on the other $16$ (it only counts their labels), and its prediction for the held-out component is scored. The estimate is (number of wrong predictions)/$17$.

steps.title: Rounds that hold out an *Accept* component ($9$ rounds)
steps.body: The training set has $9 - 1 = 8$ *Accept* and $8$ *Reject* labels. The labels are tied, so the tie-break rule makes the baseline predict *Reject*. The held-out label is *Accept*, so all $9$ of these predictions are wrong.

steps.title: Rounds that hold out a *Reject* component ($8$ rounds)
steps.body: The training set has $9$ *Accept* and $8 - 1 = 7$ *Reject* labels, so the majority is *Accept*. The held-out label is *Reject*, so all $8$ of these predictions are wrong.

steps.title: Combine and interpret
steps.body: Errors $= 9 + 8 = 17$, so the LOOCV misclassification rate is $\dfrac{17}{17} = 1$. By contrast, the baseline trained on all $17$ components always predicts *Accept* and misclassifies only the $8$ *Reject* components (training error $\tfrac{8}{17}$). Removing a component always tips the nearly balanced majority **against** that component's own label, so LOOCV is maximally pessimistic here.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: A label-count baseline cannot be perfect on data containing both labels. In fact every held-out component is misclassified.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: $\tfrac{8}{17}$ is the training (resubstitution) error of the baseline fitted on all $17$ components. It would also be the LOOCV error if ties were broken in favour of *Accept*, but the stated rule breaks ties in favour of *Reject*.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: $\tfrac{9}{17}$ counts only the errors on the held-out *Accept* components and misses that every held-out *Reject* component is also misclassified.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: All $9$ held-out *Accept* components are predicted *Reject* (tie-break) and all $8$ held-out *Reject* components are predicted *Accept* (majority), so the error is $\tfrac{17}{17} = 1$.

solution.commonTrap: Assuming that LOOCV gives about the same error as fitting on all the data ($\tfrac{8}{17}$). For a majority-vote baseline on nearly balanced labels, leaving a component out changes the training majority against that very component.

answerVerification.checkCode:
lab=['A']*9+['R']*8
err=0
for i in range(len(lab)):
    t=lab[:i]+lab[i+1:]
    pred='A' if t.count('A')>t.count('R') else 'R'  # tie -> Reject
    err+=pred!=lab[i]
print(err,len(lab),err/len(lab))  # 17 17 1.0

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: MODERATE — spotting the block-triangular structure gives the eigenvalues quickly, and the eigenvalues of the adjugate follow from adj(A) = det(A) A^{-1}; about 2 minutes.
concept: Eigenvalues of the adjugate: adj(A) = det(A) A^{-1}, so its eigenvalues are det(A)/λ for each eigenvalue λ of A.
stem:
Let

$$
A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}.
$$

The sum of the eigenvalues of $\operatorname{adj}(A)$, the adjugate (classical adjoint) of $A$, is ________. (Answer in integer)

solution.quick: The first column of $A$ is $(1, 0, 0)^{\top}$, so the eigenvalues are $1$ and those of $\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$, namely $3$ and $5$. Then $\det A = 15$ and $\operatorname{adj}(A) = 15A^{-1}$ has eigenvalues $15, 5, 3$, whose sum is $23$.

steps.title: Find the eigenvalues of $A$
steps.body:
Expanding $\det(A - \lambda I)$ along the first column, whose only non-zero entry is $1 - \lambda$:

$$
\det(A - \lambda I) = (1 - \lambda)\big[(4 - \lambda)^2 - 1\big] = (1 - \lambda)(\lambda - 3)(\lambda - 5).
$$

So the eigenvalues are $1$, $3$ and $5$.

steps.title: Relate $\operatorname{adj}(A)$ to $A^{-1}$
steps.body: $\det A = 1 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 = 15 \ne 0$, so $A$ is invertible and $\operatorname{adj}(A) = \det(A)\,A^{-1} = 15A^{-1}$. If $A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$, then $A^{-1}\mathbf{v} = \tfrac{1}{\lambda}\mathbf{v}$, and so $\operatorname{adj}(A)\,\mathbf{v} = \tfrac{15}{\lambda}\mathbf{v}$.

solution.shortcut: The sum of the eigenvalues of $\operatorname{adj}(A)$ is its trace, which equals the sum of the principal $2 \times 2$ minors of $A$ (the products of eigenvalues taken two at a time): $\det\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix} + \det\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -3 \\ 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix} + \det\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix} = 15 + 4 + 4 = 23$.
solution.commonTrap: Taking the eigenvalues of $\operatorname{adj}(A)$ to be those of $A^{-1}$ ($1, \tfrac{1}{3}, \tfrac{1}{5}$, sum $\approx 1.53$) and forgetting the factor $\det A = 15$, or reading the diagonal entries $1, 4, 4$ as the eigenvalues although $A$ is not triangular.

import numpy as np
A=np.array([[1,2,-3],[0,4,1],[0,1,4]],float)
adj=np.linalg.det(A)*np.linalg.inv(A)
print(np.round(np.linalg.eigvals(A),6),np.round(np.linalg.eigvals(adj),6),round(np.trace(adj),6))  # sum 23

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: MODERATE — four standard properties to test on a ten-edge graph; each needs one idea (an odd cycle, the number of odd-degree vertices, a cut vertex, and why a cut vertex rules out a Hamiltonian cycle); about 2.5 minutes.
concept: Graph properties: bipartiteness and odd cycles, Euler trails and vertex degrees, cut vertices, and Hamiltonian cycles.
stem:
A water utility has eight pumping stations $P, Q, R, S, T, U, V, W$ joined by ten pipelines. It is modelled as a simple undirected graph $G$ whose edges are

$$
PQ,\ QR,\ RS,\ ST,\ TU,\ UP,\ PS,\ SV,\ VW,\ WS.
$$

Which of the following statements about $G$ is/are true?

options.label: A
options.text: $G$ is bipartite.

options.label: B
options.text: $G$ has a walk that traverses every edge exactly once.

options.label: C
options.text: $G$ has a cut vertex, that is, a vertex whose deletion (together with its incident edges) leaves a disconnected graph.

options.label: D
options.text: $G$ has a Hamiltonian cycle.

solution.quick: The triangle $S, V, W$ is an odd cycle, so $G$ is not bipartite. $G$ is connected with exactly two odd-degree vertices ($P$ and $S$), so an Euler trail exists. Deleting $S$ cuts $\{V, W\}$ off from the rest, so $S$ is a cut vertex, and a graph with a cut vertex has no Hamiltonian cycle. True: (B) and (C).

steps.title: Degrees and structure
steps.body: Degrees: $P = 3$ ($Q, U, S$), $Q = 2$, $R = 2$, $S = 5$ ($R, T, P, V, W$), $T = 2$, $U = 2$, $V = 2$, $W = 2$; the sum is $20 = 2 \times 10$. The graph is the hexagon $P\,Q\,R\,S\,T\,U$ with the chord $PS$, plus the triangle $S\,V\,W$ attached at $S$. It is connected.

steps.title: (A) Bipartite?
steps.body: The edges $SV$, $VW$ and $WS$ form a cycle of length $3$. A bipartite graph has no odd cycle, so $G$ is **not** bipartite. (The hexagon with chord $PS$ alone would be bipartite, since its cycles $PQRS$, $PSTU$ and $PQRSTU$ have lengths $4$, $4$ and $6$.) (A) is false.

steps.title: (B) Euler trail
steps.body: A connected graph has a walk using every edge exactly once if and only if it has $0$ or $2$ vertices of odd degree. Here exactly $P$ (degree $3$) and $S$ (degree $5$) are odd, so such a walk exists, starting at one of them and ending at the other. One example: $P\,Q\,R\,S\,V\,W\,S\,T\,U\,P\,S$. (B) is true.

steps.title: (C) Cut vertex
steps.body: Deleting $S$ removes the edges $RS$, $ST$, $PS$, $SV$ and $WS$. The remaining graph has the component $\{V, W\}$ (edge $VW$) and the component $\{P, Q, R, T, U\}$ (the path $R\,Q\,P\,U\,T$), so it is disconnected. $S$ is a cut vertex and (C) is true.

steps.title: (D) Hamiltonian cycle
steps.body: The only edges leaving $\{V, W\}$ go to $S$. A Hamiltonian cycle that visits $V$ and $W$ must enter and leave this pair through $S$, so it would pass through $S$ twice, which is not allowed. In general, a graph with a cut vertex has no Hamiltonian cycle. (D) is false. The true statements are (B) and (C).

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: The triangle $S\,V\,W$ is an odd cycle, and a bipartite graph cannot contain an odd cycle. Only the hexagon-plus-chord part of $G$ is bipartite.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: $G$ is connected and has exactly two odd-degree vertices, $P$ (degree $3$) and $S$ (degree $5$), so an Euler trail from $P$ to $S$ exists, for example $P\,Q\,R\,S\,V\,W\,S\,T\,U\,P\,S$.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: Removing $S$ separates $\{V, W\}$ from $\{P, Q, R, T, U\}$, so $S$ is a cut vertex.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: Any cycle through $V$ and $W$ must enter and leave them through $S$, using $S$ twice. Since $S$ is a cut vertex, no Hamiltonian cycle exists.

solution.commonTrap: Declaring $G$ bipartite after checking only the hexagon and its chord, whose cycles all have even length, and missing the triangle $S\,V\,W$ hanging off $S$.

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: HARD — a complete 2×2 chi-squared test of independence in a 1-mark slot: expected counts for all four cells, the correct degrees of freedom and two critical values, with traps for omitting the 'attended' cells and for using 2 degrees of freedom; about 2.5 minutes.
concept: Chi-squared test of independence for a 2 × 2 contingency table.
stem:
A clinic compares two appointment-reminder methods. Of $180$ patients reminded by SMS, $54$ missed their appointment; of $180$ patients reminded by a phone call, $36$ missed their appointment. A chi-squared test of independence (without any continuity correction) is used to test

$H_0$: missing the appointment is independent of the reminder method.

Use the critical values $\chi^2_{0.05,\,1} = 3.841$, $\chi^2_{0.01,\,1} = 6.635$, $\chi^2_{0.05,\,2} = 5.991$ and $\chi^2_{0.01,\,2} = 9.210$, where $\chi^2_{\alpha,\,\nu}$ is the value exceeded with probability $\alpha$ by a chi-squared random variable with $\nu$ degrees of freedom.

Which one of the following statements is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The test statistic is $4.80$; $H_0$ is rejected at the $5\%$ level but not at the $1\%$ level.

options.label: B
options.text: The test statistic is $3.60$; $H_0$ is not rejected at the $5\%$ level.

options.label: C
options.text: The test statistic is $4.80$ with $2$ degrees of freedom; $H_0$ is not rejected at the $5\%$ level.

options.label: D
options.text: The test statistic is $4.80$; $H_0$ is rejected at both the $5\%$ and the $1\%$ levels.

solution.quick: Overall $90$ of $360$ patients missed, so each group's expected counts are $45$ missed and $135$ attended. $\chi^2 = \tfrac{81}{45} + \tfrac{81}{45} + \tfrac{81}{135} + \tfrac{81}{135} = 4.8$ with $(2-1)(2-1) = 1$ degree of freedom. Since $3.841 < 4.8 < 6.635$, $H_0$ is rejected at $5\%$ but not at $1\%$.

steps.title: Build the contingency table
steps.body:
| Method | Missed | Attended | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| SMS | 54 | 126 | 180 |
| Phone call | 36 | 144 | 180 |
| Total | 90 | 270 | 360 |

steps.title: Expected counts under $H_0$
steps.body: $E = \dfrac{\text{row total} \times \text{column total}}{N}$. Missed: $\dfrac{180 \times 90}{360} = 45$ in each row. Attended: $\dfrac{180 \times 270}{360} = 135$ in each row.

steps.title: Compute the statistic
steps.body:
Every cell differs from its expected count by $9$ in absolute value:

$$
\chi^2 = \frac{(54-45)^2}{45} + \frac{(36-45)^2}{45} + \frac{(126-135)^2}{135} + \frac{(144-135)^2}{135} = 1.8 + 1.8 + 0.6 + 0.6 = 4.8.
$$

steps.title: Degrees of freedom and decision
steps.body: $\nu = (r-1)(c-1) = (2-1)(2-1) = 1$. Compare with the $1$-degree-of-freedom critical values: $4.8 > 3.841$, so $H_0$ is rejected at the $5\%$ level; $4.8 < 6.635$, so it is not rejected at the $1\%$ level. (The $p$-value is about $0.028$.)

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: $\chi^2 = 4.8$ with $1$ degree of freedom lies between $3.841$ and $6.635$, so $H_0$ is rejected at $5\%$ but retained at $1\%$.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: $3.60$ comes from using only the two 'missed' cells ($1.8 + 1.8$). The two 'attended' cells add another $1.2$, giving $4.8$, which exceeds $3.841$.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: A $2 \times 2$ table has $(2-1)(2-1) = 1$ degree of freedom, not $2$. Comparing $4.8$ with $5.991$ wrongly retains $H_0$ at the $5\%$ level.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: At the $1\%$ level the critical value is $6.635$, which $4.8$ does not exceed, so $H_0$ is not rejected at $1\%$.

solution.commonTrap: Summing $(O - E)^2/E$ over the 'missed' cells only and getting $3.60 < 3.841$. All four cells of the table contribute to the statistic.

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: HARD — the gap method with an extra boundary condition that removes one gap; it is easy to over-count by ignoring the first-slot rule or to under-count by not ordering the academic speakers; about 2 minutes.
concept: Counting arrangements in which no two items of one kind are adjacent (gap method), with a restriction on the first position.
stem:
A one-day workshop has seven talks in seven consecutive time slots. Four of the speakers are from industry and three are from academia; the seven speakers are distinct people and each gives exactly one talk. The organisers require that

1. no two academic speakers speak in consecutive slots, and
2. the first slot is given to an industry speaker.

The number of possible speaking orders is

solution.quick: Order the industry speakers ($4! = 24$ ways). The academic speakers go into separate gaps, but the gap before the first industry speaker is forbidden, leaving $4$ gaps. Choose $3$ of them ($\binom{4}{3} = 4$) and order the academic speakers ($3! = 6$): $24 \times 4 \times 6 = 576$.

steps.title: Arrange the industry speakers
steps.body: Place the four industry speakers in a row first: $4! = 24$ orders. This creates $5$ gaps: $\_\,I\,\_\,I\,\_\,I\,\_\,I\,\_$.

steps.title: Apply both conditions to the gaps
steps.body: No two academic speakers may be consecutive, so each gap holds at most one academic speaker. The first slot must go to an industry speaker, so the leading gap (before the first $I$) must stay empty. That leaves $4$ usable gaps: the three between industry speakers and the one after the last.

steps.title: Place and order the academic speakers
steps.body: Choose $3$ of the $4$ usable gaps: $\binom{4}{3} = 4$ ways. The three academic speakers are distinct, so they can be ordered in $3! = 6$ ways.

steps.title: Multiply
steps.body: $24 \times 4 \times 6 = 576$. Check: without condition 2 there are $24 \times \binom{5}{3} \times 6 = 1440$ orders; those that start with an academic speaker use the leading gap plus $2$ of the other $4$, giving $24 \times \binom{4}{2} \times 6 = 864$; and $1440 - 864 = 576$.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: $96 = 4! \times \binom{4}{3}$ chooses the slots for the academic speakers but never orders the three distinct academic speakers; the factor $3! = 6$ is missing.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: $4! \times \binom{4}{3} \times 3! = 24 \times 4 \times 6 = 576$, using only the four gaps that are not before the first industry speaker.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: $864$ is the number of valid orders that **start** with an academic speaker, the complement of the required set within the $1440$ orders with no two academic speakers adjacent.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: $1440 = 4! \times \binom{5}{3} \times 3!$ ignores condition 2 and allows an academic speaker in the first slot.

solution.commonTrap: Using all five gaps of the gap method, as in the unrestricted problem. The first-slot condition removes the leading gap, which reduces $\binom{5}{3} = 10$ to $\binom{4}{3} = 4$.

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: HARD — four quantifier movements across implication and disjunction; the asymmetric rule (a universal quantifier in the antecedent becomes an existential when moved out) is counter-intuitive and has to be confirmed or refuted with a counter-model; about 3 minutes.
concept: First-order logic: moving a quantifier across implication and disjunction when the other operand has no free occurrence of the variable.
stem:
Let $P$ and $R$ be unary predicate symbols, and let $S$ be a sentence (a formula with no free variables) in which the variable $x$ does not occur. As usual in first-order logic, every interpretation has a non-empty domain. Two formulas are *logically equivalent* if they have the same truth value in every interpretation.

In which of the following pairs are the two formulas logically equivalent?

options.label: A
options.text: $\big(\exists x\, P(x)\big) \rightarrow S$ and $\forall x\, \big(P(x) \rightarrow S\big)$

options.label: B
options.text: $\big(\forall x\, P(x)\big) \rightarrow S$ and $\forall x\, \big(P(x) \rightarrow S\big)$

options.label: C
options.text: $\exists x\, \big(P(x) \rightarrow R(x)\big)$ and $\big(\forall x\, P(x)\big) \rightarrow \big(\exists x\, R(x)\big)$

options.label: D
options.text: $\forall x\, \big(P(x) \vee S\big)$ and $\big(\forall x\, P(x)\big) \vee S$

solution.quick: Rewrite $\alpha \rightarrow \beta$ as $\neg\alpha \vee \beta$ and push negations inward. A quantifier that leaves the antecedent of an implication flips: $(\exists x\,P(x)) \rightarrow S \equiv \forall x\,(P(x) \rightarrow S)$, but $(\forall x\,P(x)) \rightarrow S \equiv \exists x\,(P(x) \rightarrow S)$. So (A), (C) and (D) are equivalences and (B) is not.

steps.title: Tools
steps.body:
Use $\alpha ightarrow  eta \equiv 
eg\alpha \vee  eta$, $
eg\exists x\,\varphi \equiv  orall x\,
eg\varphi$, $
eg orall x\,\varphi \equiv \exists x\,
eg\varphi$, and $\exists x\,(\varphi \vee \psi) \equiv \exists x\,\varphi \vee \exists x\,\psi$. Because $x$ does not occur in $S$ and the domain is non-empty, $ orall x\,(\varphi(x) \vee S) \equiv  orall x\,\varphi(x) \vee S$ and $\exists x\,(\varphi(x) \vee S) \equiv \exists x\,\varphi(x) \vee S$.

steps.title: Pair (A)
steps.body:
$ orall x\,(P(x) ightarrow S) \equiv  orall x\,(
eg P(x) \vee S) \equiv  ig( orall x\,
eg P(x) ig) \vee S \equiv 
eg\exists x\,P(x) \vee S \equiv  ig(\exists x\,P(x) ig) ightarrow S$. The two formulas are **equivalent**.

steps.title: Pair (B)
steps.body: $\big(\forall x\,P(x)\big) \rightarrow S \equiv \neg\forall x\,P(x) \vee S \equiv \exists x\,\neg P(x) \vee S \equiv \exists x\,(P(x) \rightarrow S)$, with $\exists$, not $\forall$. Counter-model: domain $\{a, b\}$, $P(a)$ true, $P(b)$ false, $S$ false. The left formula is true (its antecedent $\forall x\,P(x)$ is false), but the right formula is false because $P(a) \rightarrow S$ is $\text{T} \rightarrow \text{F}$. **Not equivalent.**

steps.title: Pair (C)
steps.body:
$\exists x\,(P(x) ightarrow R(x)) \equiv \exists x\,(
eg P(x) \vee R(x)) \equiv \exists x\,
eg P(x) \vee \exists x\,R(x) \equiv 
eg orall x\,P(x) \vee \exists x\,R(x) \equiv  ig( orall x\,P(x) ig) ightarrow  ig(\exists x\,R(x) ig)$. **Equivalent.**

steps.title: Pair (D) and conclusion
steps.body: $S$ has a single truth value in a given interpretation. If $S$ is true, both formulas are true. If $S$ is false, both reduce to $\forall x\,P(x)$. So they are **equivalent**. (Contrast $\forall x\,(P(x) \vee R(x))$, which does **not** split over $\vee$, because $R(x)$ depends on $x$.) The equivalent pairs are (A), (C) and (D).

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: $\forall x\,(\neg P(x) \vee S) \equiv \neg\exists x\,P(x) \vee S$, which is $(\exists x\,P(x)) \rightarrow S$. An existential in the antecedent becomes a universal outside.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: $(\forall x\,P(x)) \rightarrow S$ is equivalent to $\exists x\,(P(x) \rightarrow S)$, not to the universal form. The domain $\{a, b\}$ with only $P(a)$ true and $S$ false makes the left side true and the right side false.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation:
$\exists x\,(
eg P(x) \vee R(x))$ splits into $\exists x\,
eg P(x) \vee \exists x\,R(x)$, which is $
eg orall x\,P(x) \vee \exists x\,R(x)$, that is, $( orall x\,P(x)) ightarrow (\exists x\,R(x))$.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: Because $x$ does not occur in $S$, the disjunct $S$ can be moved out of the scope of $\forall x$: if $S$ is true both sides are true, and if $S$ is false both sides say $\forall x\,P(x)$.

solution.commonTrap: Treating every quantifier as if it could be pulled out unchanged, which makes (B) look like (A). A quantifier moved out of the **antecedent** of an implication switches between $\forall$ and $\exists$, because the antecedent sits under a negation.
